claims.statement: HOOK: Fifty million dollars. That was the price tag on Netflix. And Blockbuster said no.
claims.evidence: All three accounts name $50M (Antioco LinkedIn Dec 2021: 'apparently offered to sell their company for $50 million'; Hastings via Marketplace 2020; Randolph's memoir). No deal happened. The hook does not use 'laughed', so it does not exaggerate.

claims.statement: PROMISE: Today, Netflix is worth hundreds of billions.
claims.evidence: Range ~$293B (mid-Oct 2026) to $450B estimate; 'hundreds of billions' is the conservative wording (verified round 2).

claims.statement: PROMISE: Blockbuster? Down to one store. In Oregon. / Today, one Blockbuster is still open. A single franchised store. In Bend, Oregon.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): 'only one franchised store remains open, located in Bend, Oregon'. The promise shorthand is fine because the aftermath says 'franchised'.

claims.statement: PROMISE: And the boardroom fight, seven years later, that nobody remembers.
claims.evidence: 2000 to 2007 = seven years, which is correct (8-K 19 Mar 2007; FY2006 release 27 Feb 2007). But 'that nobody remembers' is an absolute claim we cannot support. The fight was reported at the time (SEC filings, trade press), and even Stratrix only says 'almost nobody can name it'. The brief bans exaggeration in the hook.
claims.fix: 'And the boardroom fight, seven years later, that most retellings skip.' (or 'that almost nobody remembers')

claims.statement: Dallas, Texas. Blockbuster headquarters. The year is two thousand.
claims.evidence: Variety 2025 (via Stratrix): everyone agrees on a meeting at Blockbuster's Dallas HQ. Year 2000 is the safe wording (c14).

claims.statement: Blockbuster was born right here in Dallas, in nineteen eighty-five.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): first store opened 19 Oct 1985 in Dallas, Texas.

claims.statement: Thousands of stores. Close to five billion dollars a year in revenue. And still growing, up about eleven percent.
claims.evidence: Verified in round 1: 2000 revenue $4,960.1M vs $4,463.5M (+11.1%); ~7,677 stores at end of 2000.

claims.statement: John Antioco. Around twenty years at Seven-Eleven. Then Circle K. Then Taco Bell. In 1997, he took the top job at Blockbuster.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia Blockbuster (re-read): June 1997, Taco Bell president Antioco resigned to become CEO of Blockbuster. Career sequence verified in round 2.

claims.statement: Across the table: three visitors from California. Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph... And their finance chief, Barry McCarthy.
claims.evidence: The visitors are correct (Randolph's memoir places Hastings, Randolph and McCarthy at the table). But the line comes right after 'The boss is John Antioco', so 'Across the table' tells the viewer as fact that Antioco sat across from them. Antioco says he was not part of the meeting and only stopped by to greet the guests. The flag ('Who was in the room') only comes later, after the viewer has already pictured the scene.
claims.fix: 'In the building: three visitors from California.' (or 'Their visitors: three men from California.'). The director should not seat the Antioco silhouette at the table in this scene.

claims.statement: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, who founded Netflix in 1997.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (re-read): incorporated in Delaware in August 1997.

claims.statement: Since September 1999, one flat monthly fee.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (re-read): 'Our subscription service has grown rapidly since its launch in September 1999.'

claims.statement: By the end of the next year, about twenty-five million American homes will own a player. Nearly double. That year, Americans will spend twenty-one billion dollars renting and buying videos.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (re-read), citing Adams Media: ~25M US households at end of 2001, +91% in 2001; video rentals and purchases $21B in 2001.

claims.statement: About three hundred thousand subscribers. Revenue: thirty-five point nine million dollars. And the loss: fifty-seven point four million.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (re-read): 2000 revenue $35,894K, net loss $57,363K. S-1 via Stratrix: 292,000 subscribers at end of 2000.

claims.statement: Every version of this story agrees on that number. Almost everything else is disputed. Who was in the room. What was said. Even the month.
claims.evidence: $50M is named in all three accounts. The date is disputed: early 2000 (Hastings, Marketplace) vs September 2000 (Randolph/Wikipedia).

claims.statement: Netflix is on its way to losing more this year than its own price tag.
claims.evidence: 2000 net loss $57.4M > $50M. 'On its way' avoids the hindsight problem.

claims.statement: In two thousand, the dot-com bubble peaked and began to burst.
claims.evidence: Nasdaq peak 10 Mar 2000 (verified round 2).

claims.statement: Blockbuster's parent company is the media giant Viacom. Could Antioco buy Netflix on his own? We simply don't know.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): parent Viacom 1994-2004. Correctly framed as an open question.

claims.statement: Fifty million was about one percent of Blockbuster's yearly revenue.
A rental business with no stores. No shelves. No counters. No rent.
claims.evidence: Netflix had no retail outlets, but it did pay rent: its prospectus describes executive offices in Los Gatos, 'one primary distribution center and a series of low-cost regional distribution centers'. 'No rent' is literally false. The intended point is no store rent.
claims.fix: 'No stores. No shelves. No counters. No store rent.'

claims.statement: Antioco, LinkedIn 2021: 'I can say with complete confidence that there were never any serious acquisition talks in 2000.' He says he wasn't even in the meeting. He only stopped by to greet the guests.
claims.evidence: Verbatim match with the post of 23 Dec 2021 as quoted by Stratrix (re-read). Attributed correctly.

claims.statement: In his 2019 book, That Will Never Work, he recalls Antioco struggling not to laugh.
claims.evidence: Randolph's memoir (Vanity Fair excerpt Sept 2019; Inc. 2019). Framed as his recollection.

claims.statement: In 2023, he wrote on Twitter that Blockbuster 'laughed us out of the room.' That's how Randolph remembers it.
claims.evidence: Fortune, 14 Apr 2023: Randolph recalled on Twitter. Flagged as his memory (verified round 2).

claims.statement: Reed Hastings has reportedly said he doesn't think it was serious. More curiosity than anything else.
claims.evidence: Variety, 21 Mar 2025, via Stratrix (re-read): 'They had us down there, but I don't think it was serious. I think it was curiosity rather than anything else.' Paraphrased and hedged.

claims.statement: Three men. Three memories. Told nearly twenty years later, or more.
claims.evidence: Memoir 2019 (19 yrs), Marketplace 2020, LinkedIn 2021, tweet 2023, Variety 2025.

claims.statement: In May 2002, it goes public. $15 per share. Valued at about $310 million. Six times its Dallas price tag. The offering alone raises $82.5 million.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (re-read): dated 22 May 2002; 5,500,000 shares at $15.00 = $82,500,000; 20,648,074 shares outstanding after the offering x $15 = $309.7M = 6.2x $50M.

claims.statement: More than six hundred thousand subscribers. About double. More than eleven and a half thousand titles. $19.95 a month.
claims.evidence: Prospectus summary (re-read): 'more than 600,000 subscribers', 'more than 11,500 ... titles', '$19.95 per month'. 600k+ vs 292k = about 2x.

claims.statement: In 2004, it hits its peak. 9,094 stores. And 84,300 employees.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read), citing SEC: 'At its peak in 2004, Blockbuster employed 84,300 people worldwide and operated 9,094 stores.'

claims.statement: That same year, it splits from Viacom. And launches Blockbuster Online.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): spun off from Viacom on or around 14 Oct 2004; online DVD subscriptions introduced as Blockbuster Online.

claims.statement: January 2005. It drops most late fees.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): 'Antioco scrapped late fees in January'. 2005 10-Q: from 1 Jan 2005 at US company-operated stores (round 2).

claims.statement: [After January 2005] Then a new player arrives. Carl Icahn... He builds a stake of nearly ten percent. In May 2005, he wins a seat on the board.
claims.evidence: Wrong order after the reshuffle. Icahn's Schedule 13D on Blockbuster has an event date of 14 Dec 2004. His funds bought from 11 Nov 2004, and the Dallas Morning News called him the biggest shareholder on 28 Dec 2004. So he arrived BEFORE the January 2005 late-fee move, not after it. The ~10% stake and the May 2005 proxy win are correct (Wikipedia; NBC May 2005).
claims.fix: Replace 'Then a new player arrives. The activist investor Carl Icahn.' with 'Meanwhile, a new player has arrived. Since late two thousand and four, the activist investor Carl Icahn has been buying in.' Keep the rest: 'He builds a stake of nearly ten percent. In May two thousand and five, he wins a seat on the board.' Or move the Icahn beat before the January 2005 late-fee line.

claims.statement: For 2005: a net loss of $588 million. More than half is a write-down.
claims.evidence: FY2006 release (re-read): 2005 net loss $588.1M; $341.9M non-cash impairment of goodwill and other long-lived assets (58%).

claims.statement: In autumn 2006, Total Access. Rent online. Return the disc to a Blockbuster store. Swap it for a free rental.
claims.evidence: FY2006 release (re-read): launched about five months before Feb 2007; customers can return DVDs by mail or exchange them at a participating store 'for free in-store movie rentals'.

claims.statement: About 2.2 million online subscribers. 700,000 added in three months alone. The target: three million by the end of March. Back in profit, $54.7 million.
claims.evidence: FY2006 release (re-read): ~2.2M online subscribers at end of 2006; ~700,000 added in Q4; 'a total of 3 million BLOCKBUSTER Total Access subscribers by the end of the first quarter'; 2006 net income $54.7M.

claims.statement: Antioco says Netflix came back to the table. Serious talks, he says, in early 2007. That's his account.
claims.evidence: Antioco, LinkedIn Pulse 1 Jun 2022, via Stratrix (re-read): by early 2007 Total Access 'did trigger serious M&A discussions between the two companies'. Attributed twice.

claims.statement: January 2007. Bonus $2.28M offered; he says he's owed $7.65M. In March, they settle. Lump-sum exit payment just under five million. His old contract would have paid thirteen and a half million.
claims.evidence: FY2006 release (re-read): on 25 Jan 2007 the board 'exercised negative discretion' and awarded $2.28M; Antioco maintains $7.65M. 8-K of 19 Mar 2007 (re-read): lump sum $4.9875M 'as compared to a lump sum payment of $13.5 million' under the previous agreement. That $13.5M was conditional (termination without cause or resignation for good reason on 31 Dec 2007), so 'would have paid' is an acceptable simplification.

claims.statement: That summer, Jim Keyes takes over as CEO.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster release of 2 Jul 2007: Keyes appointed Chairman and CEO (round 2).

claims.statement: That same year, Netflix starts streaming.
claims.evidence: Watch Now launched Jan 2007 (round 2).

claims.statement: 23 September 2010, Chapter Eleven. In 2011, Dish buys it out of bankruptcy, about 1,700 stores. In early 2014, the last company-owned stores close.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (re-read): bankruptcy 2010; 'The next year, its remaining 1,700 stores were bought by ... Dish Network'; last corporate-owned stores 12 Jan 2014. Filing date 23 Sept 2010 verified in round 2.

claims.statement: In 2025, revenue of forty-five point two billion dollars. Profit: eleven billion dollars. About nine hundred times that fifty million price tag.
claims.evidence: The figures are correct. Netflix FY2025 10-K / Q4 letter: revenue $45,183M, net income $10,981M (~$11.0B). But the order is misleading: '900 times' comes straight after the profit figure, so viewers will hear the $11B profit as 900x $50M. Revenue/$50M = 904x. Profit/$50M = 220x.
claims.fix: Reorder: 'In twenty twenty-five, revenue of forty-five point two billion dollars. About nine hundred times that fifty million price tag. Profit: eleven billion dollars.' On-screen kinetic text must attach '×900' to the revenue figure, not the profit.

claims.statement: Did one no in Dallas kill Blockbuster? Probably not on its own. Blockbuster did fight for the online future. For a while, it was gaining ground. Would owning Netflix have saved it? Nobody can know.
claims.evidence: Supported by the Total Access subscriber growth (FY2006 release). The counterfactual is correctly left open. Hindsight fairness is good.

claims.statement: When a small company could replace your core business, don't just ask what it's worth today. Ask what it costs you if it wins.
claims.evidence: One lesson, no factual claim.

issues: AFTERMATH (Netflix today): 'Profit: eleven billion dollars. About nine hundred times that fifty million price tag.' Viewers will attach 900x to the profit (it is really 220x). The 900x belongs to revenue ($45.2B / $50M = 904). Fix: 'In twenty twenty-five, revenue of forty-five point two billion dollars. About nine hundred times that fifty million price tag. Profit: eleven billion dollars.' Director: put the x900 kinetic text on the revenue figure.

AFTERMATH (Icahn): 'January two thousand and five. It drops most late fees. ... Then a new player arrives. The activist investor Carl Icahn.' The order is wrong. Icahn started buying on 11 Nov 2004, and his Schedule 13D has an event date of 14 Dec 2004, so he arrived before the late-fee move. Fix: 'Meanwhile, a new player has arrived. Since late two thousand and four, the activist investor Carl Icahn has been buying in. That's an investor who buys in to shake things up. He builds a stake of nearly ten percent. In May two thousand and five, he wins a seat on the board.' (or move the Icahn beat before the late-fee line).
THE PRESSURE: 'No shelves. No counters. No rent.' Netflix did pay rent (offices in Los Gatos and distribution centers, per its prospectus). Fix: 'No shelves. No counters. No store rent.'

PROMISE (hook zone, must not exaggerate): 'And the boardroom fight, seven years later, that nobody remembers.' 'Nobody remembers' is an absolute claim we cannot support (it was in SEC filings and the press). Fix: 'And the boardroom fight, seven years later, that most retellings skip.' (or 'that almost nobody remembers').

SET THE SCENE: 'Across the table: three visitors from California.' This comes right after 'The boss is John Antioco', so it presents as fact that Antioco sat across from them, which he disputes (he says he only greeted the guests). Fix: 'In the building: three visitors from California.' Director: do not seat the Antioco silhouette at the pitch table; keep him a separate figure until the 'three memories' beat.
notes: Round 3 (remake v2). Re-opened this round: the Netflix 424B4 prospectus (c1, c4, c5-c7, c9, c10, c49, plus the facilities that disprove 'No rent'), the Blockbuster FY2006 release of 27 Feb 2007 (c29-c32, c34 bonus), the Blockbuster 8-K of 19 Mar 2007 (c34 settlement), Stratrix with its Antioco/Hastings/Variety/Marketplace quotes (c13-c16, c19, c52), the Wikipedia Blockbuster article (c20, c21 incl. 84,300 employees, c24, c27, c28, c33, c39-c41), the Icahn Schedule 13D, event date 14 Dec 2004 (c33 order), and Netflix FY2025 results via SEC search (c42: revenue $45,183M, net income $10,981M). The six new uses the writer asked about (c20, c21, c9, c10, c30, c42) are all correct. Only the placement of 900x next to the profit is a problem. The hook (no 'laughed', '$50M price tag', 'said no') and the re-hooks ('Remember that number', 'here's where it gets interesting/strange', 'that's not the crazy part', 'almost everyone skips', 'plays its best card') do not overstate facts, except 'that nobody remembers' (issue 4). Quotes: the Antioco LinkedIn line is verbatim; Randolph's two quotes are framed as his memory; Hastings is paraphrased with 'reportedly'. The apocryphal Apollo 13 story and 'dot-com hysteria' are correctly left out. Structure: hook, promise, scene, fairness section, freeze with comment prompt at ~3:24 of ~8:20 (~40%, close enough to the midpoint), reveal, numbers, verdict line 'Blockbuster PASSED', one lesson, teaser. ~1,320 words, about 8:20 at speed 1.15. That is in the 8-10 min range, but if the voice runs faster than about 165 wpm it drops under 8:00; the director can hold beats on the counters. All five fixes are wording changes; the story holds up, so no reject. After the fixes, a quick diff check is enough for a pass. Housekeeping for @researcher (not blocking): in research.md, mark c33 as verified (13D, NBC) with 'stake built from Nov 2004', and change c10's date to 'prospectus 22 May 2002, delivery 29 May 2002'.
